title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks - Guidance
author: Ari Chen
summary: Consolidated guidance and standards for SRE teams at Redwood Inference covering SLO definitions and templates, error budget policy, capacity planning methodology, reliability initiatives and incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and canonical runbooks.
body:
Purpose
This document defines Redwood Inference SRE guidance for: SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and runbooks. It is intended for service owners, on-call SREs, product engineering leads, and platform teams.

Scope
- Applies to all customer-facing inference and control-plane services (hosted API, dedicated control-plane, console, and private deployment control plane).
- Excludes experimental internal prototypes; those should follow the lightweight SLO process in the Experimental Services playbook.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets
Overview
Establish service-level objectives (SLOs) for the user-visible aspects of each service. SLOs are the primary reliability target; error budgets quantify acceptable failure and guide releases and capacity decisions.

SLO types (examples)
- Availability: % successful requests over rolling 30d and 90d windows. Typical target: 99.95% for critical production endpoints.
- Latency: P50 / P95 / P99 for key API routes. Example targets: P95 < 120ms, P99 < 500ms for short text generation; batch/long-run routes may have higher targets.
- Throughput/Throttle: sustained RPS and token/sec targets for dedicated pools. Example: per-dedicated-pool 24-hr throughput target at 90% of reserved capacity.
- Correctness/Quality: evaluation-based checks (e.g., model response quality measured on canary prompt sets) with regression thresholds.

SLO template (must be filled per-service)
- service_name: short identifier (e.g., inference-public-v1)
- owner: team + primary oncall
- user_impact: short description of who is affected
- objective: numeric SLO(s) and measurement window (e.g., Availability: 99.95% over 30d)
- indicator: monitoring metric(s) (e.g., http_success_ratio{route=\"/v1/generate\"})
- measurement_window: 30d / 90d
- alert_thresholds: warning (error budget burn > 25% in 7d), critical (burn > 50% in 24h)
- error_budget_policy: permitted mitigation actions, rollout constraints, auto-throttle settings

Error budget policy (standard)
1. Calculate error budget: error_budget = 1 - objective. Example: for 99.95% SLO, monthly allowable errors = 0.05% of requests.
2. Track burn-rate on rolling windows (24h, 7d, 30d).
3. Trigger tiers:
   - Tier 1 (Watch): burn > 10% of monthly budget within 7d - engineering lead notified, prepare rollback plan.
   - Tier 2 (Action): burn > 25% in 7d OR > 10% in 24h - freeze risky releases, reduce traffic to new model variants/canaries, enable additional caching/batching.
   - Tier 3 (Escalate): burn > 50% in 24h OR budget consumed - immediate incident declaration and oncall-led mitigation (rollback/fallback).
4. Release gating: if error budget consumed > 25% in 7d, canary progression requires explicit SRE sign-off. If consumed > 50%, halt all non-critical rollouts until remediation and postmortem.

2) Capacity Planning
Principles
- Plan for steady-state + headroom for spikes. Headroom target = 2x expected P99 daily peak for public hosted API (subject to cost tradeoffs) or 1.2-1.5x for dedicated pools depending on SLA and contract.
- Use demand-driven provisioning: horizontal scaling where possible; vertical sizing for GPU pools must consider model memory/KV cache needs.
- Prefer autoscaling with conservative cooldowns, combined with reserved baseline capacity for predictable workloads.

Process (quarterly planning + event-driven updates)
1. Demand forecasting: aggregate historical RPS, tokens/sec, model mix, and per-route latency and queue metrics. Use 90/95/99 percentile traffic projections.
2. Capacity model: map forecasted token/sec to GPU instance types using per-model throughput profiles (see Quantization Profiles doc). Maintain a capacity matrix: {region, instance_type, pool_size, expected_rps, safety_headroom}.
3. Cost vs. risk analysis: quantify cost of additional reserved capacity vs. expected error budget burn cost. Include committed contracts for Dedicated customers.
4. Run capacity tests quarterly: synthetic load test (k6 / internal harness) and production canary surge (low-traffic window) to validate autoscaling and throttles.

Capacity thresholds and alerts (example)
- Utilization warning: GPU util > 70% sustained for 1h (per-pool)
- Critical: GPU util > 85% for 15m or queuing latency growth > 2x baseline
- Preemptive alert: predicted capacity shortfall within 48h based on traffic projection and model rollout schedule

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization
Objective-driven roadmap
- Maintain a quarterly reliability roadmap mapped to SLOs. Each initiative must include target SLO impact, owner, expected effort, and rollback criteria.
- Typical initiatives: adaptive batching, KV-prefix caching improvements, model quantization rollouts, autoscaler tuning, multi-region fallbacks, and improved retry/backoff strategies.

Evaluation and validation
- Use controlled canaries with the evaluation harness and prompt sets for quality regression detection. Tie canary results to error budget impact estimates before global rollout.
- Validate performance gains with A/B tests (latency and cost) and include cost-per-token metrics in the initiative metrics.

4) Incident Review Standards
Blameless, timely, and actionable
- Declare incidents per Incident Process (see oncall-and-incident-response). For SLO-impacting incidents, the timeline must be published within 24h.
- Postmortem requirements (published within 5 business days):
  1. Summary and impact (users affected, SLOs hit, duration)
  2. Timeline with timestamps and contributing factors
  3. Root cause analysis (not just symptoms)
  4. Action items, owners, and ETAs (categorized as short/medium/long term)
  5. Follow-up verification plan and tests to confirm resolution
  6. Error budget accounting and implications for rollouts/releases
- Postmortem review: SRE lead and service owner must review within 10 business days and mark actions as accepted or assign to owners.

Incident review checklist (must be completed)
- Was the SLO affected? If yes, quantify burn and add to team\'s error budget ledger.
- Were runbooks followed? If not, document why and update the runbook.
- Monitoring and alerting gaps identified? Create tickets for missing metric/alert coverage.
- Communication audit: confirm status page, customer-facing comms, and internal comms timelines.

5) Operational Tooling Requirements
Monitoring and dashboards
- Each SLO must have a single canonical dashboard showing: indicator metric, SLO target line, rolling burn rates (24h/7d/30d), and related KPIs (latency distributions, traffic mix, cache hit rates, GPU pool utilization).
- Dashboards must be live in the central Grafana folder: /dashboards/sre/slo-<service_name>.

Alerting and noise control
- Alerts mapped to SLO tiers (watch/action/escalate). Alerts should include runbook links and required first actions.
- Implement alert suppression during planned maintenance windows and automated suppression when safe fallbacks are active.

Tracing and debugging
- Distributed tracing must be enabled for all API routes. Capture sampling of payloads only with appropriate PI/PII filtering.
- Include traceable request IDs in logs and surface request ID in customer-facing error responses where appropriate.

Runbooks and playbooks
- Runbooks must be concise, step-by-step, and kept under 2 pages where possible. Include: symptoms, immediate mitigation steps, escalation path, safe rollback steps, and verification queries.

6) Canonical Runbooks (examples)
A. High P99 Latency for /v1/generate
- Symptoms: P99 latency > 2x baseline for > 10m while traffic steady.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Check GPU pool utilization, queue length, and per-node memory pressure.
  2. If util > 85% or queuing increased, scale up pool (manual + autoscaler override) and enable model fallback variant with lower memory/throughput if available.
  3. Enable additional batching conservatively: adjust batch timeout from 8ms -> 12ms for latency-sensitive routes.
  4. If latency persists, revert recent model rollout or routing change.
- Escalation: page inference-oncall -> SRE lead.
- Post-incident: update runbook with root cause and verification queries.

B. GPU Node OOM / GPU-side OOM Errors
- Symptoms: recurring OOM errors across nodes or a sudden increase in OOM logs.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Drain the affected node from the pool (mark as unschedulable).
  2. Check recent model variants deployed to the pool and per-model memory stats.
  3. If caused by a new model variant, rollback the variant and trigger a controlled canary with memory-limited instances.
  4. If caused by memory leak, restart runtime processes on the node and run extended profiling (collect heap/KV cache stats).
- Escalation: page infra-sre and serving-runtime owners.

C. Control-plane DB High Write Latency
- Symptoms: increased write latency > 2x baseline, backlog in request queue, failed persistence operations.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Enable write-backoff and reduce non-critical background jobs.
  2. Scale read-replicas and promote healthy replicas for read-heavy operations.
  3. If persistent, fail fast non-essential writes and surface degraded mode to customers via status page.

7) Ownership, Review Cadence, and Documentation Standards
- Ownership: each SLO and runbook must have a named owner (primary oncall + engineering manager). Owners are responsible for keeping content current and ensuring dashboards/alerts exist.
- Review cadence: SLO definitions and runbooks reviewed at least quarterly and after any incident that exercised the runbook.
- Documentation style: confluence pages must be clear, include links to dashboards/alerts, include example queries (PromQL/SQL), and short CLI snippets for common actions (kubectl/drain, scaling).

Appendices
A. Example PromQL queries
- Availability: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=~\"inference.*\",status!~\"5..\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=~\"inference.*\"}[5m]))
- Error budget burn rate (7d): (1 - availability_7d) / (1 - objective)

B. Example alert policy snippets (pseudo-YAML)
- name: SLO_Burn_Watch
  metric: slo_burn_rate_7d{service=\"inference-public-v1\"}
  condition: > 0.10 for 1h
  severity: warning
  runbook: \"/confluence/eng-sre/sre-slos-capacity-and-runbooks-2025-11-10.json#Error-budget-policy\"

C. Radiosilence windows and planned maintenance
- All planned maintenance windows must be registered in the central calendar and set maintenance flag in monitoring at least 48h prior. Suppress SLO alerts during approved windows and record impact for the next SLO review.
